Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- German zookeepers in Nuremberg will bottle-feed a four-week-old polar bear and rear it away from its mother after concerns the mother would eat her cub, officials said Thursday. Zookeepers fear the unnamed polar bear cub could be at risk of being eaten. The cub, which doesn't yet have a name, was being cared for at Nuremberg City Zoo, where it was resting under heat lamps and is drinking formula. "It's gaining weight, it's very hungry, it drinks a lot of milk," said Alexandra Foghammar, a spokeswoman for the city. The zoo announced Thursday that the cub is female. Wednesday, the zoo said keepers decided to take the cub away from its mother, Vera, because the mother was showing signs of being upset and confused, taking her baby in and out of the animals' enclosure. "We were 100 percent sure that the baby was going to die if we didn't take it away from her," Nuremberg zoo director Dag Encke told Time magazine. "This would have been a death verdict for the cub." The zoo confirmed earlier this week that its other female polar bear, Vilma, had eaten her two offspring. The zoo said it feared Vera would do the same, so it took her cub away as a precaution. Since then, the cub is thriving in the care of humans, but Vera seems to miss her cub, Foghammar said.  Watch how zoo has faced criticism over polar bears. » . "The mother is a little bit nervous," she said. "She walks around and is searching for the baby, but the responsible persons for the zoo say this is normal. It will continue for three or four days. It's a normal situation." The zookeepers are pondering whether to bring another adult bear, possibly the cub's father, Felix, to the zoo to help Vera overcome her loss, and are seeking another small bear to serve as a companion for the rescued cub, Time reported. The zoo said a keeper entered Vilma's enclosure Monday and noticed that her two cubs were nowhere to be found. The zoo said it assumes Vilma ate her young because she believed the cubs were sick, though zookeepers say the cubs were last seen on Sunday and appeared in good health. But Foghammar told Time that the separation of the bears was bad for the "principle of wildlife conservation" at the zoo: "Now the cub will not grow up to act in a natural way, just as the mother lacked the experience to bring up a cub." The plight of the cub follows the case last year of Knut, a cub rejected by its mother at Berlin Zoo who became the focus of a media frenzy after animal rights campaigners called for it to be killed, claiming it had become too dependent on humans. Caretakers are feeding it a specially formulated milk substitute every few hours, mimicking the frequent nursing schedule the cub would have received from its mother.

"The little one is stable but remains in a critical phase," a zoo spokesperson said. "Polar bear cubs are extraordinarily vulnerable in their first weeks of life. We are cautiously optimistic, but the coming days will be decisive."

Their eyes typically open at around one month of age, and they are unable to walk until roughly three months old. Survival rates for hand-reared cubs have historically been low, though advances in veterinary care have improved the odds in recent years.

## The Mother's Behavior

Zoo officials emphasized that the mother's abandonment of the cub is not unusual among polar bears, particularly first-time mothers or animals in captivity. In the wild, it is not uncommon for a mother to abandon or even reject a cub she senses may not survive, redirecting her energy toward future reproduction.

"This kind of behavior, while difficult to witness, is part of the natural instinct of the species," the spokesperson explained. "The mother is otherwise healthy and behaving normally. There is no indication she was ill or distressed beyond her decision to stop caring for the cub."

Keepers said the mother has since returned to her usual routine and remains under observation.

In previous years, the facility has reported cubs that did not survive their first weeks despite intervention, underscoring the persistent challenges of breeding and rearing the Arctic predators in captivity.

Knut became an international sensation and a symbol of both conservation efforts and the ethical debates surrounding hand-rearing wild animals. He died in 2011 at the age of four from a brain condition.

Animal welfare advocates have periodically criticized the practice of hand-rearing, arguing that cubs raised by humans can struggle to develop natural behaviors. Zoo officials counter that intervention is justified when the alternative is the certain death of the animal.

## Keepers Hand-Rear Orphaned Polar Bear as Experts Question Intervention

**By Staff Reporter**

A tiny polar bear cub, rejected by her mother days after birth, has become the center of a heated debate among conservationists, animal welfare advocates, and zoo staff over whether human intervention undermines the very wildlife principles zoos claim to uphold.

The female cub, unnamed pending a public vote, now spends her days wrapped in warming blankets inside a climate-controlled nursery, where keepers bottle-feed her a specialized formula every three hours around the clock.

Zoo officials say the mother, a first-time parent, showed no interest in nursing after the birth—a not-uncommon occurrence among captive polar bears.

"When a mother rejects her cub, we face an impossible choice," said the zoo's head of carnivore care. "We can let nature take its course, or we can step in. We chose to give this cub a chance at life."

Staff report the cub is gaining weight steadily and responding well to hand-rearing, though they acknowledge the road ahead remains uncertain.

### The Controversy

Not everyone agrees the intervention was appropriate.

Critics argue that hand-reared polar bears often struggle to develop natural behaviors, may become improperly imprinted on humans, and are unlikely to ever contribute to species survival in the wild.

"There's a real tension here," said an independent wildlife biologist not affiliated with the zoo. "Bottle-feeding a charismatic cub generates enormous public affection and, frankly, ticket sales. But we have to ask honestly whether we're serving conservation or simply serving our own emotional needs."

Some conservation organizations maintain that resources devoted to hand-rearing a single non-releasable animal might be better spent protecting wild populations and their rapidly shrinking Arctic habitat.

### The Zoo Responds

Zoo leadership pushed back against the criticism, emphasizing the cub's role as an "ambassador animal."

"This cub may never live in the wild, and we're honest about that," a spokesperson said. "But she can inspire millions of people to care about polar bears and the climate threats facing them. That awareness translates into real support for wild conservation efforts."

The zoo also noted that the cub's care follows established welfare protocols and international breeding-program guidelines.

### An Uncertain Future

For now, the cub remains behind the scenes as keepers monitor her health. Officials say a decision about her long-term placement will come in coming months, guided by recommendations from a coordinated species-management program.

Whatever the outcome, the small bear has already reignited a question the zoo world continues to grapple with: where the line falls between compassion for an individual animal and the broader mission of protecting a species.
